qs: Do you work or are you a student?

I'm working at the moment. I moved to Rome a few years ago, and I currently work for a small company that deals with clients from China, so a lot of my day is spent translating emails and arranging meetings. It's quite demanding, but I enjoy the variety.
What do you like most about your job?

Probably the fact that no two days are the same. One day I might be dealing with a supplier, and the next I'm helping a customer with a tricky problem. It keeps me on my toes, and I've picked up a lot of practical skills along the way.
Is there anything you would like to change about your job?

If I'm honest, I'd like a bit more flexibility. At the moment I have to be in the office every day, which means quite a long commute. Even one day a week working from home would make a big difference to my work-life balance.
Do you plan to keep doing this job in the future?

For the next few years, yes, but in the long run I'd like to move into something more international. That's actually one of the reasons I'm preparing for IELTS, because a lot of the roles I'm interested in require a strong level of English.
Where is your hometown?

I come from Shanghai, on the east coast of China. It's one of the biggest cities in the country, and it's famous for its waterfront, where you can see historic European-style buildings on one side of the river and very modern skyscrapers on the other.
What do you like about your hometown?

I love how lively it is. There's always something going on, whether it's a new exhibition, a food market or a concert. The public transport is excellent too; you can get almost anywhere by metro, which is something I really miss now that I live in Rome.
Has your hometown changed much since you were a child?

Enormously. When I was little, many people still lived in traditional lane houses, but a lot of those neighbourhoods have been redeveloped. The city is much cleaner and more convenient now, although I do feel that some of its old character has been lost.
Would you like to live there in the future?
Possibly, but not right now. I'm enjoying the experience of living abroad and learning a new language. That said, I'd never rule it out, because my family is there and it will always feel like home.
Do you live in a house or a flat?

I live in a flat in Rome, in a fairly old building near the city centre. It's on the third floor, and like a lot of buildings here it doesn't have a lift, so I get plenty of exercise carrying my shopping upstairs.
What is your favourite room in your home?
Definitely the kitchen. It's quite small, but it gets a lot of sunlight in the morning, and that's where I spend most of my free time, either cooking or studying at the little table by the window.
What would you like to change about your home?

I'd love a bit more space, to be honest. Rents in central Rome are very high, so I've had to compromise on size. If I could change one thing, I'd add a small balcony where I could grow some herbs and sit outside in the evenings.
Do you plan to live there for a long time?

Probably for another year or two. It's convenient for work and I like the neighbourhood, but if my circumstances change, I might move somewhere a little further out, where I could get more space for the same rent.
What is your daily routine like?

On weekdays it's fairly predictable. I get up at around seven, have a quick coffee and some breakfast, and then commute to work. I usually finish at six, and in the evening I try to fit in an hour of English or Italian before dinner.
Do you prefer mornings or evenings?

I'm definitely more of a morning person. My mind feels clearer early in the day, so I try to do anything that requires concentration then. By the evening I'm usually too tired to take in anything new.
Has your routine changed recently?

Yes, quite a lot. Since I started preparing for IELTS, I've cut down on the time I spend on my phone in the evenings and set aside regular slots for studying. It took a while to get used to, but now it feels natural.
Is it important to have a routine?

I think so, at least for me. Having a routine means I don't waste energy deciding what to do next, and it helps me make steady progress. Having said that, it's also nice to break it occasionally, for example by doing something spontaneous at the weekend.
What kind of food do you like?

I've got quite a broad taste in food, but my favourite is probably still Chinese home cooking, especially the dishes my mother makes. Since moving to Italy, though, I've also become a big fan of simple Italian dishes like pasta with fresh tomatoes.
Do you often cook at home?

Yes, most days. Eating out in Rome is lovely but it adds up quickly, so I cook dinner at home most evenings. I usually make something quick, like a stir-fry or a bowl of pasta, and I cook a bigger meal at the weekend.
Is there any food you don't like?

I'm not keen on very sweet desserts. I find that a few spoonfuls are enough, and anything more makes me feel a bit sick. I also struggle with blue cheese, which is a shame because some of my friends here love it.
Have people's eating habits changed in recent years?

Definitely. People eat a lot more convenience food now, and delivery apps have made it incredibly easy to order a meal without leaving the sofa. At the same time, more people seem to be paying attention to healthy eating, so it's a bit of a mixed picture.
What's the weather like where you live?

Rome has a typical Mediterranean climate, so summers are long, hot and dry, and winters are mild, with quite a lot of rain. It hardly ever snows, which is quite different from the winters I'm used to in China.
What's your favourite season?

I'd say autumn. The temperature is just right, neither too hot nor too cold, and the light in the late afternoon is beautiful. It's also the season when the city gets a bit quieter after the summer tourists leave.
Does the weather affect your mood?

To some extent, yes. A sunny day definitely lifts my spirits, and I'm more likely to go for a walk or meet friends. On grey, rainy days I tend to stay in and feel a bit less motivated, although that's a good time to catch up on studying.
Has the weather in your country changed in recent years?

People certainly say it has. Summers in many parts of China seem to be getting hotter, and extreme weather like heavy flooding seems to happen more often. I think most people now see it as a sign of climate change.
How do you usually travel around your city?

Mostly by metro and bus. Rome's metro network is quite limited compared with Shanghai's, so I often have to combine it with a bus. When the weather's nice, I sometimes walk, because the city centre is fairly compact.
Is public transport good in your city?

It's reasonable, but it's not always reliable. Buses can be crowded and delays are quite common, especially at rush hour. On the plus side, a single ticket lasts a hundred minutes, so changing between buses and the metro is quite cheap.
Do you prefer public transport or driving?

Public transport, without a doubt. Driving in central Rome is stressful, and finding a parking space is almost impossible. On the bus or the metro I can listen to podcasts or review vocabulary, so the journey isn't wasted.
How could public transport be improved?

The most important thing would be more frequent and reliable services. Real-time information at bus stops would also help a lot, because at the moment you're never quite sure when the next bus will turn up.
Do you like reading?
Yes, very much, although I don't read as much as I used to. These days I mostly read on my e-reader during my commute, which is a great way to make use of time that would otherwise be wasted.
What kind of books do you like reading?

I tend to go for non-fiction, especially books about history and psychology. I like learning something new from what I read. Every now and then, though, I enjoy a good detective novel, just to switch off.
Do you prefer paper books or e-books?

For convenience, e-books win hands down. I can carry hundreds of books in my bag and look up words instantly, which is really useful when I'm reading in English. But for books I really love, I still like to own a paper copy.
Do you think people read less than they used to?

In terms of books, probably yes, because there's so much competition from videos and social media. But in a way people read more than ever; they just read short posts and messages rather than long texts, which isn't quite the same thing.
Do you like listening to music?
I do. I usually have music on in the background while I'm cooking or cleaning, and I always listen to something on long journeys. It helps me relax and makes boring tasks feel a lot shorter.
What kind of music do you listen to?

My taste is quite varied. I listen to a lot of Chinese pop, but I've also got into Italian songs since I moved here, partly because they help me with the language. When I need to concentrate, I put on some instrumental music.
Did you learn a musical instrument as a child?

I had piano lessons for a few years in primary school, but I have to admit I wasn't very dedicated. I stopped when I started secondary school, and now I can only remember a couple of simple pieces, which I slightly regret.
Should children learn music at school?

Yes, I think it's valuable. Learning an instrument teaches patience and discipline, and playing in a group helps children work together. It doesn't have to be about becoming a professional musician; it's more about enjoying something creative.
How often do you use your mobile phone?

Far too often, if I'm honest. I use it for almost everything: work emails, messaging my family, paying for things and studying. I've recently started using a screen time app to keep my usage under control.
What do you mainly use it for?
Communication, mostly. Since my family is in China, video calls are really important to me. I also use it a lot for learning, for example vocabulary apps and podcasts, so it's not all wasted time.
Could you live without your phone for a day?

I could, but it would be harder than I'd like to admit. I'd probably feel a bit lost without maps and messages. Actually, I think it would be a good experiment to try once in a while, just to see how much I really need it.
Should children have smartphones?

I think it depends on their age. For teenagers, a phone can be useful for safety and keeping in touch. For younger children, though, I'd be more cautious, because they can easily get hooked and spend too much time on screens.
How many languages can you speak?

Apart from Chinese, I speak English fairly well, and I'm learning Italian because I live in Rome. My Italian is still at a basic level, but I can manage everyday situations like shopping or going to the doctor.
Why are you learning these languages?

English is mainly for my career and for the IELTS exam, since I'd like to have more international options in the future. Italian is more about daily life; living here without it would be really limiting.
What is the most difficult part of learning a language?

For me it's speaking with confidence. I can understand much more than I can say, and when I'm under pressure my mind sometimes goes blank. The only real solution is to practise speaking as much as possible, even if I make mistakes.
Is it better to learn a language in the country where it's spoken?

Generally, yes. Being surrounded by the language forces you to use it in real situations, which speeds things up enormously. Having said that, you still need to study grammar and vocabulary systematically, otherwise you can pick up bad habits.
What do you usually do at weekends?

It varies, but I usually do a bit of shopping and cleaning on Saturday morning, and then I try to get out of the house. I might visit a museum, go for a long walk in one of Rome's parks or meet friends for dinner.
Do you prefer to spend weekends alone or with others?

A mix of both. I need some time on my own to rest and catch up on things, but I also like to see friends at least once over the weekend. Otherwise the week can feel a bit lonely, especially when you live abroad.
What did you like to do at weekends as a child?
My parents often took me to the park on Sunday mornings, and afterwards we'd have dim sum at a local restaurant. It was a simple routine, but it's one of my happiest childhood memories.
Do people have enough free time these days?

Not really. Many people work long hours, and even when they're off, their phones keep them connected to work. I think people need to be more deliberate about protecting their free time, for the sake of their health.

part2.card: Describe a skill you learned as an adult.
part2.zh: 成年后学会的一项技能
points: when and where you learned it
and explain how this skill has helped you.
answer: I'd like to talk about learning Italian, which is probably the most useful skill I've picked up as an adult.

I started about a year and a half ago, shortly before I moved to Rome. At first I just used a couple of phone apps, but I soon realised that wasn't enough, so once I arrived I signed up for an evening course at a local language school. I also made a point of using Italian in everyday situations, like ordering coffee or asking for directions, even when people could have answered me in English.

The hardest part, at least at the beginning, was the grammar. Italian verbs change their endings depending on who is doing the action and when, and there are lots of irregular forms that you simply have to memorise. Pronunciation was easier than I expected, although I still struggle with the rolled r.

As for how it's helped me, it has made a huge difference to my everyday life. Things like dealing with my landlord, going to the doctor or sorting out my residence permit used to be really stressful, but now I can handle most of them on my own. It has also helped me make friends with my neighbours, which has made Rome feel much more like home.

More generally, learning a language as an adult has taught me to be patient with myself. Progress isn't always obvious from one week to the next, but when I look back over a few months, I can see how far I've come, and that's really motivating.
phrases: make a point of doing sth
p3: Is it easier for children or adults to learn new skills?
What skills will be most important in the future?
Should employers pay for their staff to learn new skills?

part2.card: Describe a city you have visited that you would like to visit again.
points: and explain why you would like to visit it again.
answer: The city I'd like to describe is Florence, in central Italy. It's only about an hour and a half from Rome by high-speed train, and I went there for a long weekend last spring with two friends.

We spent most of our time just wandering around the historic centre, which is surprisingly compact, so you can walk almost everywhere. We visited the cathedral, with its enormous red-brick dome, and on our second day we queued for ages to get into the Uffizi Gallery, which has an incredible collection of Renaissance paintings. In the evenings we ate in small family-run restaurants, and I tried the famous Florentine steak, which was absolutely huge.

What I remember most, though, is climbing up to a square on a hill just outside the centre at sunset. From there you get a breathtaking view over the whole city, with the dome in the middle and the hills of Tuscany in the background. It was one of those moments when you just stand there and take it all in.

The main reason I'd like to go back is that we really only scratched the surface. There are dozens of museums and churches we didn't have time to see, and I'd love to explore the countryside around the city, maybe visit a vineyard or one of the smaller hill towns. I'd also like to go in a quieter season, because in spring it was extremely crowded, and I think the city would be even more enjoyable without so many tourists.
p3: Why do people like to visit famous cities?
What problems can tourism cause for historic cities?
How can cities balance the needs of tourists and residents?

part2.card: Describe a person who has had an important influence on you.
part2.zh: 一个对你影响很大的人
points: and explain how they have influenced you.
answer: I'd like to talk about my English teacher in high school, Mr Zhang, who probably influenced me more than any other teacher I've had.

He taught our class for three years, from the age of fifteen until we finished school. He wasn't the kind of teacher who tried to be popular. In fact, at first a lot of us found him quite strict, because he expected us to speak English in every lesson and he never accepted homework that was handed in late. But over time we realised that he genuinely cared about every student in the class, including the ones who were struggling.

What made him special was the way he made English feel like a real language rather than just an exam subject. He used to bring in songs, newspaper articles and clips from films, and he encouraged us to argue about them in English. I remember being terrified the first time I had to give my opinion in front of the class, but he was very patient and never made anyone feel stupid for making mistakes.

In terms of his influence on me, I think he's the main reason I became interested in other cultures and decided to live abroad. He also taught me that making mistakes is part of learning, which is something I remind myself of now that I'm learning Italian and constantly getting things wrong. Even today, when I'm preparing for IELTS, I sometimes think about what he would say if he saw my essays.
phrases: feel like a real language rather than just an exam subject
感觉是真正的语言，而不只是考试科目
p3: What qualities make a good teacher?
Do teachers have more influence on children than parents do?
Will technology ever replace teachers?

part2.card: Describe a piece of technology you find useful.
part2.zh: 一件你觉得有用的科技产品
points: and explain why it is useful to you.
answer: The piece of technology I want to talk about is a translation app on my phone, which I use almost every day.

I first downloaded it when I was planning my move to Italy, about two years ago. At that time I couldn't speak a word of Italian, so I was worried about how I'd cope with things like renting a flat or opening a bank account. The app turned out to be a lifesaver.

What makes it so useful is that it does much more than translate single words. I can point my phone's camera at a document or a sign and the translation appears on the screen almost instantly, which is incredibly handy when I'm dealing with official letters or reading labels in the supermarket. It also has a conversation mode, where two people take turns to speak and the app translates out loud. I used that a lot in my first few months, for example at the doctor's or when a technician came to fix the boiler.

These days I rely on it less than I used to, because my Italian has improved, and I try not to use it as a crutch. I find that if I always reach for my phone, I don't make the effort to remember new words. So now I mainly use it to check things I'm not sure about, or for official documents where I really can't afford to make a mistake.
Overall, I'd say it has made settling into a new country far less stressful than it would otherwise have been.
phrases: turn out to be a lifesaver
p3: Do people rely too much on technology?
Will machine translation make learning languages unnecessary?
How has technology changed the way people communicate?

part2.card: Describe a book you enjoyed reading.
points: and explain why you enjoyed it.
answer: The book I'd like to talk about is Sapiens by Yuval Noah Harari, which is a short history of humankind. I read it about three years ago, mostly on long train journeys, and it's one of the few books I've finished and then immediately recommended to all my friends.

As the title suggests, it covers the whole story of our species, from the time when several kinds of humans lived side by side to the modern world of science and global trade. What makes it different from a typical history book is that it focuses on big ideas rather than dates and battles. For example, the author argues that humans became so successful because we can cooperate in large numbers by believing in shared stories, such as money, nations and laws.

I enjoyed it for a few reasons. First of all, it's very readable. The author explains complicated ideas in plain language, with lots of surprising examples, so it never feels like hard work. Secondly, it made me look at everyday things differently. After reading it, I couldn't help thinking about how much of what we take for granted is based on agreements between people rather than on anything physical.

Not everyone agrees with its arguments, and some historians think it oversimplifies things. But for me that's part of its appeal, because it got me thinking and discussing the ideas with other people. I actually read part of it again in English last year as reading practice, which was a good challenge.
phrases: focus on big ideas rather than dates and battles
关注大观点，而不是年代和战争
it never feels like hard work
p3: Do young people read less than older people?
What are the benefits of reading fiction?
Should schools make students read classic books?

part2.card: Describe a time when you helped someone.
part2.zh: 一次你帮助别人的经历
points: and explain how you felt about it.
answer: I'd like to describe a time last autumn when I helped a Chinese student who had just arrived in Rome.

I met her by chance at a post office, where she was trying to send off her application for a residence permit. She was clearly confused, because the forms were all in Italian and the queue behind her was getting longer and longer. I remembered how stressed I'd been in exactly the same situation, so I offered to help.

First, I went through the forms with her and explained what each section meant, and then I showed her which documents she needed to attach. It turned out that she was missing a copy of her passport, so we went to a nearby shop to make one before she lost her place in the queue. After that, I gave her my number and told her to get in touch if she had any problems. She messaged me a few more times over the next few weeks, mostly about opening a bank account and registering with a doctor, and I explained what I'd done when I went through the same process.

I felt really good about it, partly because it was so easy for me to help, but it made a big difference to her. It also made me realise how much I've learned since I arrived. A couple of years ago I was the one who felt lost, and now I'm able to guide someone else. We've actually stayed in touch, and we sometimes meet for coffee, so I gained a friend as well.
phrases: lose your place in the queue
p3: Why are some people unwilling to help others?
Should children be taught to help others at school?
Do people help their neighbours less than in the past?

part2.card: Describe a place where you like to relax.
part2.zh: 一个你喜欢放松的地方
points: and explain why it is a good place to relax.
answer: The place I'd like to talk about is Villa Borghese, which is a huge park in the middle of Rome, just a short walk from where I live.

I go there at least once a week, usually on Sunday mornings, and sometimes after work in the summer, when it stays light until late. It used to be the private gardens of a wealthy family, and it's full of old trees, fountains and little lakes, so it doesn't feel like you're in the middle of a capital city at all.

What I do there depends on my mood. Sometimes I just walk along the shady paths and listen to a podcast, and other times I take a book and sit on the grass for an hour or so. There's a small lake where you can hire a rowing boat, which I've done a couple of times with friends, and there's also a terrace on the edge of the park with a wonderful view over the rooftops of the city.

I think it's a good place to relax for two main reasons. First, it's a real escape from the noise and traffic of Rome, which can be quite overwhelming, especially in summer. As soon as I walk through the gates, I feel calmer. Second, it gives me a chance to disconnect from my phone and my studies. During the week my mind is always busy, so having a regular place where I can slow down really helps me recharge for the week ahead.
phrases: doesn't feel like you're in the middle of a capital city
一点也不像在首都市中心
p3: Why do many people find it hard to relax nowadays?
Should cities have more green spaces?
Do young and old people relax in different ways?

part2.card: Describe a memorable journey you have made.
points: and explain why it was memorable.
answer: I'd like to talk about an overnight train journey I took from Rome to Sicily last summer, which was one of the most unusual trips I've ever made.

I went with a friend who was visiting me from China. We could have flown, which would have been quicker and probably cheaper, but we'd read that the train actually crosses the sea on a ferry, and we thought that sounded like too good an experience to miss.

We left Rome in the evening and had a small sleeper compartment with two bunk beds. It was quite cramped, but it was fun, and we spent the first few hours chatting and watching the countryside go by until it got dark. Early the next morning, the train reached the southern tip of the mainland, and then something amazing happened: the carriages were split up and loaded onto a ferry. We were allowed to get off the train and go up on deck, so we watched the sun rise over the sea as we crossed to Sicily, with the coast of the island getting closer and closer.

The reason it was so memorable is that the journey itself became part of the holiday, rather than just a way of getting from A to B. Normally travel is something you want to get over with as quickly as possible, but this felt like an adventure. It also made me realise that slower ways of travelling can be much more rewarding, and since then I've tried to take the train whenever I can.
phrases: too good an experience to miss
从一个地方到另一个地方
尽快把（不想做的事）做完
p3: Do people travel more than in the past?
Is air travel bad for the environment?
What could governments do to encourage people to travel by train?

part2.card: Describe a festival that is important in your country.
part2.zh: 你的国家一个重要的节日
points: and explain why it is important.
answer: The festival I'd like to talk about is the Spring Festival, or Chinese New Year, which is by far the most important celebration in China.

It's based on the lunar calendar, so the date changes every year, but it usually falls in late January or February. The celebrations traditionally last about two weeks, from New Year's Eve until the Lantern Festival, although most people only get around a week off work.

The heart of the festival is family. Hundreds of millions of people travel back to their hometowns, which is often described as the largest annual migration in the world, so trains and planes are packed. On New Year's Eve, families get together for a big dinner, and in the north it's traditional to make dumplings together. Many people also watch a long variety show on television that has been broadcast every year since the eighties. Children receive red envelopes with money inside, and in the days that follow people visit relatives and friends to wish them a happy new year.

I think it's important for two reasons. Firstly, it's the one time of year when even the busiest people make the effort to go home, so it keeps family ties strong in a society where many people live and work far from their parents. Secondly, it connects people with tradition. Even in big modern cities, customs like putting up red decorations or eating particular foods for good luck are still widely observed. Since I moved to Italy I've celebrated it with Chinese friends here, but it's never quite the same as being at home.
phrases: falls in late January or February
it's never quite the same as
p3: Are traditional festivals becoming less important?
Why do many young people enjoy celebrating Western festivals?
Should governments spend public money on festivals?

part2.card: Describe a time when you had to wait for something.
part2.zh: 一次你不得不等待的经历
points: what you did while you were waiting
and explain how you felt about waiting.
answer: I'd like to talk about the time I had to wait for my first residence permit after I moved to Italy, which tested my patience more than anything else I can remember.

The process started at the post office, where I sent off my application, and then I had an appointment at the police headquarters to have my fingerprints taken. I was told the permit would be ready in about two months, but in the end it took almost five. The problem was that during that time I only had a receipt to show that I'd applied, and some offices didn't want to accept it, so simple things like signing a phone contract became complicated.

While I was waiting, I tried to make good use of the time. I checked the status of my application online every few days, which probably didn't help my stress levels, but I also threw myself into learning Italian, because I knew that would make my life easier whatever happened. I also joined an online group of foreigners in the same situation, and sharing our experiences made me feel much less alone.

To be honest, I found the waiting really frustrating at times, mainly because I had no control over it and nobody could tell me exactly when it would be ready. Looking back, though, I think it taught me to be more patient and to focus on the things I could actually change. When I finally picked up the permit, it was a huge relief, and I remember celebrating with a very large pizza.
phrases: make good use of the time
p3: Are people less patient than they used to be?
In what situations do people often have to wait in your country?
How can organisations make waiting less unpleasant?

part2.card: Describe a goal you would like to achieve in the future.
part2.zh: 一个你将来想实现的目标
points: what you need to do to achieve it
and explain why it is important to you.
answer: One goal I'm working towards at the moment is getting an overall score of 8 in the IELTS exam, which I'm planning to take next autumn.

I set this goal a few months ago, after thinking carefully about my career. I'd like to move into a more international role in the future, and many of the jobs and courses I'm interested in ask for a high level of English. A band 8 would also be a personal milestone, because it would show that I can use English with real precision in an academic or professional setting.

To achieve it, I need to be very disciplined. I've made a study plan that covers all four skills, and I try to follow it every day, even if it's only for forty minutes. For listening and reading, I'm working through practice tests and keeping a record of every mistake, so I can see which question types I find difficult. Speaking and writing are harder to improve on your own, so I write at least one essay a week and record myself answering speaking questions, then listen back and note where I hesitate or repeat words.

The goal matters to me partly for practical reasons, but also because I enjoy the challenge. I'm learning Italian at the same time, which means my time is limited, so I have to be efficient. If I manage to reach my target, I think it'll prove to me that with a clear plan and consistent effort, I can achieve quite ambitious things.
p3: Is it important for people to set goals?
Do young people have different goals from older people?
Should parents set goals for their children?

part2.card: Describe an interesting conversation you had with someone you didn't know.
part2.zh: 一次和陌生人的有趣交谈
points: and explain why it was interesting.
answer: I'd like to describe a conversation I had a few months ago with an elderly man I met on a regional train from Rome to a small town in the hills nearby.

I was going there for a day trip, and the man sitting opposite me noticed that I was reading an Italian grammar book. He asked me, in Italian, where I was from, and when I said China, his face lit up, because it turned out he had worked in Shanghai for a few years in the nineties as an engineer.

We ended up talking for the whole hour of the journey. He told me about how different Shanghai looked back then, with far fewer skyscrapers and lots of bicycles, and I told him how much it has changed since. He also gave me some advice about learning Italian, which was simply to watch old Italian films with subtitles, because people in them speak clearly. He spoke slowly for me, and when I didn't understand something, he would act it out with his hands, which made us both laugh.

The reason I found it so interesting is that it showed me two cities I know well through a completely different pair of eyes. It was fascinating to hear what Shanghai was like when I was a small child, from someone who saw it as a foreigner, just as I'm now seeing Rome as a foreigner. It was also a real confidence boost, because it was the first time I'd had a long conversation entirely in Italian. When we got off the train, he wished me luck, and I've followed his advice about the films ever since.
phrases: through a completely different pair of eyes
p3: Do people talk to strangers less than in the past?
Should children be taught not to talk to strangers?
Why do some people find it hard to start a conversation?
